Period: The early church, first century AD
Origin: The Judaizers were Jewish Christians who insisted that Gentile converts must be circumcised and keep the Law of Moses to be saved. They appear in Acts and Galatians as a pressure group within the early church, not as an outside sect — which is why the fight over them was so painful.
Beliefs: They believed God's covenant with Israel still bound every believer: circumcision, Sabbath, food laws, and festivals were not optional customs but the terms of belonging. To them, a gospel without the Law was a gospel cut from its roots.
Practices: They traveled to Gentile churches, taught circumcision, questioned Paul's apostleship, and pressed converts to adopt Jewish observance. Their campaign reached Galatia, Antioch, and Corinth, and forced the church's first great council.
Role: Judaizers were the conservative wing of the Jewish church: sincere, Scripture-quoting, and convinced they were defending Moses. Their strength was real — they could point to centuries of covenant history — and their challenge forced the apostles to define the gospel itself.
RelationshipToJesus: Jesus never meets a Judaizer — the party arose after the resurrection — but the issue was his own: whether the kingdom he announced belonged to Israel alone or to all nations. Paul's answer, defended at the Jerusalem Council and thundered in Galatians, was that faith in Christ, not circumcision, makes a person God's own, and that requiring the Law for salvation emptied the cross.
Summary: The Judaizers were Jewish Christians who insisted Gentile converts be circumcised and keep the Law to be saved — the conservative wing whose challenge forced the church to define the gospel at the Jerusalem Council.
